# NetworkService

- Inherits [`Instance`](instance.md)
- A **service**: get it with `game:GetService("NetworkService")`
- **Not creatable**: it cannot be created with `Instance.new`

Reports the role of this process in a networked game, and joins, hosts and leaves matches.

Use `Authority` to decide whether this machine makes gameplay decisions: `if NetworkService.Authority then`. A single-player game is also an authority, so the same code works with and without networking.

`Join`, `Host` and `Disconnect` change the role at run time, at a safe point between two ticks, and `State` reports the current stage. `Authority` can change during a run: it becomes false after joining and true again after leaving. Code that runs for the whole game should listen for changes to `State` instead of reading `Authority` once.

The command-line flags `--host`, `--serve` and `--join=` make the same calls before the first tick. `--serve` is the only way to run a dedicated server.

This page lists the members this class declares. Inherited members are
listed on the page of the class that declares them.

## Properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Authority` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether this process decides the state of the world. It is true in single-player, when hosting and on a dedicated server, and false on a client, which shows the state it is sent. |
| `Channel` | `number` | — | read-only | Which channel of its world this server is: 1 for a world without channels, and for the first of a world with them. A `[[world]]` with `channels = true` in `servers.toml` is copied into channels 2, 3 and on as the open ones fill, each a server of its own. |
| `JoinCode` | `string` | — | read-only | The code other players use to join this machine's match through a relay. It is eight letters and digits, without 0, 1, I or O, which are easily confused. The relay resolves it to this host wherever the host is, including behind a home router or on a mobile network.<br><br>It is empty until `RelayState` is `Ready`, and on a machine that is not hosting through a relay. It stays the same for as long as the match is hosted, even if the relay restarts, and changes the next time `Host` is called. |
| `LocalPlayer` | `Player?` | — | read-only | The player at this machine. It exists from startup in single-player, when hosting and when joining. It is nil on a dedicated server. |
| `MaxPlayers` | `number` | `0` | read/write | The largest number of players in this machine's match, including the host's own player. It is the limit on the length of `GetPlayers()`. The host sets it, to an integer of at least 1, before or after calling `Host`.<br><br>A player who tries to join a full match is refused, and their `JoinFailed` reports that the match is full. Lowering the value removes no one: players already in the match stay until they leave or are removed with `Player:Kick`.<br><br>The value cannot exceed the capacity the match was opened with, which is 32 other players or the `--max-players` flag; that capacity is what it reads while hosting if it was never set. On a machine that joined a match it reads 0, and setting it raises an error. |
| `PeerCount` | `number` | — | read-only | The number of connected peers, not counting this process. On an authority it is the number of clients; on a connected client it is 1. |
| `Port` | `number` | — | read-only | The port of this machine's match: the port it hosts or serves on, or the port it joined. It is 0 when there is no match. A host can show it with `GetLocalAddresses` for others to join. |
| `RelayState` | `Enum.RelayState` | — | read-only | The state of this machine's match with its relay. It is `None` when there is no relay or no hosted match, `Connecting` until the relay answers, `Ready` once the relay has registered the match, and `Unreachable` while the relay does not answer. `RelayStateChanged` fires when it changes. |
| `ServerTick` | `number` | — | read-only | The authority's tick number. On the authority it is its own tick; on a client it is the newest tick the client has applied; in single-player it is 0. It counts ticks and is not a time. |
| `State` | `Enum.NetworkState` | — | read-only | The connection state of this machine: `Offline`, `Connecting`, `Connected`, `Hosting`, `Serving` or `Reconnecting`. |
| `Topology` | `Enum.NetworkTopology` | — | read-only | The network role this process runs in. For gameplay decisions, use `Authority`; this property is for showing the role, for example in a menu. |

## Methods

### `AddLocalPlayer(): Player?`

Adds a guest player to an offline game on this machine and fires `PlayerAdded`. Returns nil on a dedicated server or while connected to a match. A guest's id is valid for the session only and is not a platform account. The game decides how many local players it allows, and assigns each one's input with `InputContext.Player`. Local guests cannot join online matches.

### `CheckAction(player: Player, name: string): boolean`

Whether this player may do the action now, by the rate `DefineAction` gave it, counted by the simulation's clock. True takes one; false is logged as a suspicion (`action_over_rate`), and what to do about it is the game's. Raises an error for an action never defined.

### `DefineAction(name: string, rule: { PerSecond: number, Burst: number? })`

Says how often each player may do one of the game's own actions: `PerSecond` of them a second, up to `Burst` at once (1 when not given). Said again for the same name, it replaces the first. `CheckAction` then counts each player's.

### `Disconnect()`

Leaves the match, or stops hosting, and returns to single-player in the current scene. Server scripts start again from the beginning, because this machine is the authority again. `Disconnected` fires. A dedicated server cannot call it.

### `ForgetServerKey(address: string)`

Forgets the key this machine saved for the server at `address`, written as for `Join`. The first time a machine joins a server by its address, it saves the server's key, and a later join to the same address with another key fails with `JoinFailed`: someone may be in the way. A server whose owner reinstalled it has a new key too. A game can offer the player a way to trust it again: call this, then `Join`.

Joining by code saves nothing, so there is nothing to forget.

### `GetChannelsAsync(): { { Channel: number, Players: number, MaxPlayers: number } }`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Returns the open channels of the world this server is, each with how many players it holds and may hold, as the manager last heard. It waits for the manager's answer. For a world without channels, the one entry is this world.

### `GetLocalAddresses(): {string}`

Returns this machine's IPv4 addresses on its local networks, best first. A host can show them for players on the same network to type.

Only interfaces that are up are listed. Loopback and link-local (169.254) addresses are left out, as are virtual adapters that can be identified, such as those of a hypervisor or a container. Private ranges come first, and among them the interface of the default route. The list does not depend on a match, is not replicated, and is empty when the machine has no network.

### `GetLocalPlayers(): {Player}`

Returns the local players on this machine in the order they joined, with the primary player first. Players that are being removed are not included.

### `GetPlayers(): {Player}`

Returns every player in the game, in the order they joined. In single-player it returns the one local player, so code that loops over players works with and without networking.

### `GetStats(): { Ping: number, Jitter: number, Loss: number, SnapshotsPerSecond: number, CorrectionsPerSecond: number, Corrections: number, LastCorrection: number, PredictedDrift: number, PredictedDriftPart: BasePart?, InputBufferDepth: number, InputStarvations: number, InputReanchors: number, InterpolationDelay: number, PredictedParts: number, ResimulationsPerSecond: number, ResimulatedTicksPerSecond: number, ResimulationTime: number, UnreliableSent: number, UnreliableReceived: number, UnreliableDropped: number, BytesSent: number, BytesReceived: number, WireBytesSent: number, WireBytesReceived: number, Deferred: number, BudgetUsed: number, SwarmBytes: number, SnapshotBytes: number, AttributeBytes: number, RemoteBytes: number, UnreliableBytes: number, InputBytes: number, CrossWorldDropped: number, Path: string, LocalPlayers: { { UserId: number, Corrections: number, CorrectionsPerSecond: number, LastCorrection: number } } }`

Returns statistics about the connection, as a table. Use them to show a connection quality indicator. Every number is 0 in single-player. On an authority, the link numbers are those of the worst client and the deepest input queue.

Link quality:

- `Ping`: the round trip, in milliseconds.
- `Jitter`: how much the round trip varies.
- `Loss`: the share of packets lost, in percent.
- The number of snapshots per second.
- `Corrections`: how often this machine's own character was corrected, per second and in total since joining. `LastCorrection` is how far the last correction moved it, in meters.
- `PredictedDrift`: how far the parts this machine predicts were from the authority's at the last answer, in meters, whether or not that was a correction. These are what its character pushes and the vehicle it drives. A driven vehicle is left a few centimeters of drift and pulled back gently, so this stays small but is rarely zero. `PredictedDriftPart` is the part that was furthest, or nil.
- `InputBufferDepth`: how many ticks of this player's input the authority has queued. `InputStarvations` counts the times the queue ran empty, and `InputReanchors` the times it was restarted because the player's clock jumped, as after a long frame.
- `InterpolationDelay`: how far in the past other players are drawn, in milliseconds. It is two snapshot intervals plus the link's jitter, and adapts to the link.
- On a client, `PredictedParts` is the number of loose parts near its character that it predicts. The table also reports how often a correction made the client simulate them again, how many ticks it simulated again, and `ResimulationTime`, the average time that took in milliseconds.

Traffic: `BytesSent` and `BytesReceived` are totals since the session began. Five more fields break the total down, sent and received together: `SnapshotBytes` for world state, `AttributeBytes` for attributes, `RemoteBytes` for `RemoteEvent`s and `RemoteFunction`s, `UnreliableBytes` for `UnreliableRemoteEvent`s, and `InputBytes` for a client's input and the state of the parts it owns. `SwarmBytes` is the positions of replicated swarms. The remainder is instances being created and removed, terrain and the handshake. To get a rate, read a field twice, one second apart, and subtract.

`CrossWorldDropped` counts `CrossWorldService` messages this world dropped unheard: too many waiting, or older than 10 seconds when their turn came.

`WireBytesSent` and `WireBytesReceived` are what the network itself carried: the same messages with the transport's headers, acknowledgements, resends and encryption added. They are what a player's connection pays for, and are larger than `BytesSent` and `BytesReceived`.

On an authority, `Deferred` counts the updates its players' budgets held back in the last second (`Player.ReplicationBudget`), and `BudgetUsed` is how much of those budgets that second's snapshots spent, from 0 to 1; above 1 when what may not wait, such as a player joining, spent more. Both are 0 on a client.

`Path` says how the other end is reached: `"lan"` on the same network, `"direct"` across the internet, or `"relayed"` through a relay, which adds the relay's distance to the round trip. On a host it is the longest path among its players. It is empty when nobody is connected.

`LocalPlayers` has one entry for each local player on a machine that joined a match: the primary player first, then the guests. Each entry has the player's `UserId` and the three correction numbers for that player's character alone. It is empty on an authority and in single-player.

### `Host(port: number? = nil, options: { Relay: string? }? = nil)`

Makes this machine the authority of a match that others can join, on `port` (7777 by default), keeping the current scene. A dedicated server cannot call it.

With a relay, from `options.Relay = "host:port"` or `[network] relay`, the match is registered with the relay, and players anywhere can join it with `JoinCode`, with no port opened on a router. Hosting does not wait for the relay or depend on it: `RelayState` reports the relay's state, and the match can always be joined by address.

### `IsMuted(player: Player): boolean`

Whether the server console has muted this player (`mute`), by their account where the game named one, else by their key. What a mute stops, such as chat or voice, is the game's to decide.

### `Join(address: string? = nil, options: { Relay: string?, Direct: boolean?, Ticket: string? }? = nil)`

Connects to a server at `address`, written as `host` or `host:port`. With no address, it connects to `[network] server` from `project.toml`. Joining replaces this machine's scene with the server's, and server scripts stop, because this machine is no longer the authority. `Connected` or `JoinFailed` fires with the outcome. A dedicated server cannot join.

`address` can also be a join code, when a relay is known from `options.Relay` or `[network] relay`. A code is accepted as a player types it: in either case, with spaces or a dash. The relay is asked for the host, and the best available path is used automatically: the same network, a direct connection across the internet, or the relay. `GetStats().Path` reports which. Set `options.Direct` to false to always go through the relay. `relay://host:port/CODE` gives the relay and the code in one string. To connect to a host whose name could be read as a code, include its port.

`options.Ticket` is what this player presents to be let in: a ticket the game's backend signed when they logged in. It travels inside the encrypted connection, and the server's `OnJoinRequest` reads it.

### `PingRelayAsync(relay: string? = nil, timeout: number? = nil): { Ping: number, Matches: number, Relayed: number, BytesPerSecond: number, Uptime: number }?`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Measures the round trip to a relay and returns what the relay reports, or nil if it did not answer. Use it before hosting or joining to choose among relays in several regions.

`relay` is `host:port`; if omitted, the project's `[network] relay` is used. The method yields until the relay has answered three requests sent a tenth of a second apart, or until `timeout` seconds have passed (1.5 by default).

The result has `Ping`, the shortest of the three round trips in milliseconds; `Matches`, the matches registered with the relay; `Relayed`, the players it is relaying; `BytesPerSecond`, its traffic; and `Uptime`, in seconds. It does not need a match and does not disturb one, and several relays can be pinged at once from separate tasks.

### `RegisterAsync(address: string, name: string, password: string): { Ok: boolean, Ticket: string?, Reason: Enum.SignInFailure?, RetryAfter: number }`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Makes an account at an online game's servers and signs this player in to it, as `SignInAsync` does. A login name is 3 to 20 of the letters A to Z, the digits, `_`, `.` and `-`; two names that differ only in case, or in `l`, `I` and `1` or `o` and `0`, are one name, and the second is `Taken`. A password is 8 to 128 bytes. What the game shows a player as, with accents or other scripts, is a display name of the game's own, not the login name.

### `RemoveLocalPlayer(player: Player): boolean`

Removes a guest player from an offline game, firing `PlayerRemoving`. Returns whether the removal was started. It does not remove the primary local player or a remote player.

### `ReportSuspicion(player: Player, kind: string, detail: string?)`

Writes a line in the suspicion log, beside those the engine writes when a player goes past a limit. The server console's `suspects` and `suspect` read it, and `/metrics` counts it by `kind`. Nothing is done to the player by it.

### `SignInAsync(address: string, name: string, password: string): { Ok: boolean, Ticket: string?, Reason: Enum.SignInFailure?, RetryAfter: number }`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Signs this player in to an account at an online game's servers, and returns a ticket to join with. Call it on the player's machine, then pass the ticket to `Join`: `NetworkService:Join(address, { Ticket = result.Ticket })`.

`address` is the game's front door, `host` or `host:port`. The password crosses the network only encrypted, to the server this machine met before at that address, and is never kept. The method yields until the server answers, and never raises for a refusal: `Ok` is false and `Reason` says why. A wrong name and a wrong password are the same reason, `WrongNameOrPassword`, and take the same time, so nobody learns which names have accounts. A ticket is good for one join within 90 seconds.

### `SwitchChannel(player: Player, channel: number): boolean`

Sends `player` to channel `channel` of the world this server is, for a channel menu: as `Travel` does, and with `TravelArrived` there. A channel that is not open, or full, leaves them where they are, and a warning says why. Only a world a manager started can call it. Returns whether `player` was asked to go: false for a player who has left.

### `Travel(player: Player, target: string, data: any? = nil): boolean`

Sends `player` to another world of the game: `target` is a world's name from `servers.toml`, or an instance's `Id`. Their machine leaves this world and joins that one, which fires `TravelArrived` with `data` and the name of this world. `data` is anything `SaveService` can store, at most 16 KiB. Their character does not travel; the target spawns one.

Only a world a manager started can send players elsewhere: anywhere else, and for a world the manager does not have, this raises at once.

Returns whether `player` was sent. A player who left while the script waited, for `CreateInstanceAsync` say, is not an error: they are gone, nothing is sent, and it returns false.

### `TravelGroup(players: {Player}, target: string, data: any? = nil): {Player}`

Sends several players to the same world together, as `Travel` sends one. The target fires `TravelArrived` for each, in the order given.

Returns the players sent, in the order given. Any who left while the script waited are skipped, not an error, and the rest still go together; when none is left, it returns an empty table and sends nobody.

### `TravelToPlayer(player: Player, key: string): boolean`

Sends `player` to the world, and the channel of it, where the player whose `PublicKey` is `key` is now: a friend, a party's leader. When that world is full, or the other player is in none, they stay where they are, and a warning says why. Returns whether `player` was asked to go: false for a player who has left.

### `VerifyTicket(ticket: string): { [string]: any }?`

Checks a ticket the game's backend signed, on the server and with no call out, and returns its claims, or nil. The ticket is a standard JWT signed with Ed25519 (`EdDSA`), which any backend's JWT library issues. A ticket is accepted when its signature checks against `ticket_public_key` under `[network]` in `project.toml`, its `aud` is this game's `[project] id`, it lives at most 90 seconds between `iat` and `exp` and has not expired, and its `jti` has not been seen before by this server. Clocks may differ by 30 seconds each way.

The algorithm is never the ticket's to choose: one that says anything but `EdDSA`, including `none`, is refused before its signature is looked at, and a key the ticket names is ignored. What was wrong is written to the server's log, never told to the player. The claims are the ticket's top-level strings, numbers and booleans: `sub`, the account, and whatever else the backend put in.

## Events

Signals are deferred: a handler runs at the next resumption point, not
inside the call that fired the signal.

### `Announced(text: string)`

Fires on every machine of the match when the server's operator says something to everybody, with the console's `say` or as `stop` counts down. The engine writes it to the log and draws nothing: a game shows it its own way, or mounts `@engine/announcements`, which shows each one across the top of the screen for a few seconds.

### `ChannelMerging(seconds: number)`

Fires on a channel the manager is about to merge into another, because it has held under a quarter of its players for a while. In `seconds` its players are moved, all together, to the fullest channel with room. A game can say so first.

### `Connected()`

Fires when a join succeeds and this machine is in the server's match.

### `Disconnected(reason: string)`

Fires when the connection ends and this machine is back in single-player. The server left, the network failed, or `Disconnect` was called.

### `HostFailed(reason: string)`

Fires when `Host` cannot open its port, for example because another program is using it. This machine stays as it was. The reason is passed as readable text.

### `JoinFailed(reason: string)`

Fires when a join fails. This machine stays in single-player, in the state it was in before `Join` was called, so the menu that called `Join` is still there to handle the event.

The reason is passed as readable text: the server did not answer, the server is full, it runs a different version, or it is taking no more players from this machine's network address. Players behind one router or one mobile network share an address, and a server allows 64 of them by default (`[network] max_connections_per_address` in `project.toml`, or `--max-per-address` for a dedicated server; 0 is no limit). With a join code, it can also be that the relay did not answer, no match has that code, the host has blocked this machine, or no connection could be established in time.

### `PlayerAdded(player: Player)`

Fires when a player joins. A script that connects at its top level and then loops over `GetPlayers()` handles each player exactly once.

### `PlayerRemoving(player: Player)`

Fires when a player is leaving. The player object is still valid inside the handler, so a game can save that player's data.

### `Queued(position: number, estimateSeconds: number?)`

Fires on a client waiting in line at a full game's front door, with its place and an estimate. The place counts from 1. The estimate is about how many seconds until its turn, measured by how fast the line moved in the last five minutes, and nil before anybody has left it. It fires when the machine joins the line and every five seconds after; `Connected` fires as usual when it is let in. `@engine/travelscreen` shows it.

### `RelayStateChanged()`

Fires when `RelayState` or `JoinCode` changes: the relay registered the match, stopped answering, or started answering again. Read the two properties for the new values.

### `TravelArrived(player: Player, data: any, origin: string, reason: string)`

Fires on the server of the world a player traveled to, after `PlayerAdded`, with the `data` the world they left sent and that world's name. A player who came through the front door fires it too, with nil and an empty origin. `reason` is empty, or `"InstanceFailed"` for a player sent back because the instance they were in stopped without closing: the game can say so, and give back what the run cost.

### `TravelStarted(world: string)`

Fires on a client when it is sent to another world, by the front door or by the world it is in, before it leaves, with that world's name. Show a loading screen here and take it down on `Connected`, which fires when the next world has taken this machine; `@engine/travelscreen` is one, mounted in one line.

## Callbacks

A callback is a function that a script assigns and the engine calls. Each
callback holds one function, and assigning nil removes it.

### `OnJoinRequest = function(joiner: { PublicKey: string, Address: string, Ticket: string, AccountId: string? }): boolean, string?`

Called on the server for everybody who joins, before they are a player, to say whether they may. Return true to let them in, or false and the words they are shown. `joiner` has their `PublicKey`, their `Address` and the `Ticket` their game presented, empty for none; set `joiner.AccountId` to the account they are, usually the `sub` of `VerifyTicket`'s claims.

It runs on a thread of its own and may yield, to ask the game's backend; after 10 seconds it is a refusal, and so is an error in it. While it runs the joiner has no `Player` and is sent nothing. An account already playing is dropped when the same account joins again, and an account banned with the console's `ban` is refused after this has named it. With no `OnJoinRequest`, everybody is let in. Set it once, in a server script: a second assignment replaces the first, and a client cannot set it.
